title: India's Largest State Just Launched a Wellness Policy to Turn Varanasi and Ayodhya Into Global Ayurveda Hubs. Your Next Trip Home Could Include a Panchakarma Prescription.
excerpt: Uttar Pradesh's AYUSH Health and Wellness Policy 2026 is India's most ambitious bet on wellness tourism yet. For NRIs spending $3,000 on a weekend spa in Sedona, the same money in Varanasi will get you a month of traditional medicine with a lineage older than Western civilisation.
body:
Your mother has been telling you about the healing power of Ayurveda for decades. Now the government of India's most populous state is betting $689 million that she was right.

Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has ordered the fast-track implementation of the AYUSH Health and Wellness Policy 2026 — the most comprehensive state-level wellness policy India has ever produced. The policy will build certified Ayurveda, yoga, naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and homeopathy centres across the state, with a particular focus on turning Varanasi, Ayodhya, and Mathura into globally recognised wellness destinations.

For the Indian diaspora, this is not a government press release. It is a travel itinerary.

## What the Policy Actually Does

The AYUSH Wellness Policy 2026 does four things that have never been attempted at this scale in a single Indian state.

First, it establishes quality standards for wellness centres. Every Panchakarma centre, yoga retreat, and Ayurvedic clinic operating under the policy will need to meet certification requirements that bring them closer to international accreditation standards. The unregulated roadside "Ayurveda clinic" that made you nervous on your last trip home is exactly what the policy is designed to replace.

Second, it opens the door to private investment. The policy explicitly encourages private-sector participation in building wellness infrastructure — hotels with in-house Ayurveda wings, yoga retreat campuses with international-grade facilities, and Panchakarma centres that meet the expectations of someone who has spent 20 years in the US healthcare system.

Third, it integrates AYUSH with modern management. This means electronic health records for traditional treatments, standardised intake protocols, and outcome tracking. The goal is to make Ayurveda legible to the Western-trained physician your NRI patient is also seeing back in New Jersey.

Fourth, it ties wellness directly to tourism infrastructure. Varanasi, Ayodhya, and Mathura are already among India's most visited religious cities. The policy layers wellness services on top of existing pilgrimage infrastructure, creating a reason to stay longer and spend more.

## The Global Context

India's AYUSH sector exported $689 million in products in 2026, with new trade deals signed with Oman and New Zealand. The country's wellness tourism market is growing at double digits, driven by Kerala's established Ayurveda circuit, Goa's yoga retreats, and Uttarakhand's Himalayan meditation centres.

But Uttar Pradesh has largely sat out the wellness tourism boom. Varanasi receives millions of visitors for Ganga Aarti and temple darshan, but few of them stay for a two-week Panchakarma detox. Ayodhya's new Ram Mandir has turned it into a mega-destination, but the city's wellness infrastructure is minimal. The AYUSH policy is designed to change that calculus.

CM Yogi has also ordered the fast-tracking of integrated AYUSH colleges in five UP divisions — Mirzapur, Gonda, Meerut, Agra, and Basti — to train the workforce the wellness centres will need. This is not a pilot programme. It is industrial-scale capacity building.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

The global wellness economy is worth $5.6 trillion. Americans alone spend $4.4 trillion on healthcare annually, and a growing segment of that spending is flowing to integrative and traditional medicine. Ayurveda, yoga, and meditation are no longer fringe interests — they are mainstream wellness categories in every major US city.

But the prices are American. A week-long Panchakarma retreat in the US costs $3,000 to $8,000. A comparable programme in Varanasi — with practitioners who trained in the tradition, not a weekend certification course — costs a fraction of that. The gap is not quality. It is infrastructure and accessibility. The UP policy addresses both.

For NRIs planning summer trips home, the calculation is simple. You are already buying the plane ticket. You are already taking two weeks off. If Varanasi or Ayodhya can offer a certified, standards-compliant Panchakarma or yoga programme that your Western doctor can understand and your insurance company might one day cover, the medical tourism arbitrage is enormous.

India's National AYUSH Mission has been running since 2015, but its impact has been uneven. UP's policy is the first to explicitly target the international wellness market, with standards designed to attract foreign patients and diaspora visitors. If it works, expect every other state to follow.

## The Fine Print

The policy is a directive, not yet a regulation. Implementation timelines are vague. Private investment will take years to build the facilities the policy envisions. And the quality-control problem in Indian traditional medicine — practitioners with questionable credentials, products with inconsistent formulations, centres with no hygiene standards — will not be solved by a policy document alone.

But the direction of travel is clear. India is moving from treating Ayurveda as cultural heritage to packaging it as a clinical service with export potential. For a diaspora that has spent years defending grandmother's turmeric milk to sceptical colleagues, the vindication is arriving in the form of government policy, international trade deals, and a $689 million export industry.

Your next trip to Varanasi might include a Panchakarma prescription. Your mother would approve.
author: Diaspora Desk
